title: The autopsy
lede: Tap a cause to see the evidence. The percentages are our editorial weighting. The evidence under each one is sourced.

causes.title: The PlayStation 2, before and after it arrived
causes.text: Sony’s console reached U.S. stores on October 26, 2000 with DVD playback and EA’s games.[^7][^20] Sega’s annual report says the Dreamcast “lost significant momentum during the all-important pre-Christmas sales season.”[^2] Moore’s account: sales were “just not going to be enough to get the critical mass to take on the launch of PS2.”[^6]

causes.title: A parent that could not fund a long war
causes.text: Net losses of ¥35.6 billion, ¥42.9 billion and ¥42.9 billion in the three years to March 2000, then ¥51.7 billion.[^1][^2] Bellfield said Sega announced $100 million of launch marketing and doubted it spent half; that is his recollection, not a reported figure.[^7] Moore recalled the console selling at $199 and costing “probably” $250 to $260 to make.[^9]

causes.title: No Electronic Arts, and a trust deficit
causes.text: EA published nothing for the machine. Bing Gordon and Bernie Stolar give different reasons, but agree on the result.[^7] Stolar also describes retailers who “really hated Sega” after the Saturn.[^7]

causes.title: The home market never came
causes.text: Japan bought 950,000 consoles in fiscal 2000 and 470,000 in fiscal 2001, against 1.78 million in the United States that year.[^1][^2] Sega’s report blamed “a maturing of the market” in Japan.[^1]

causes.title: Piracy and the disc format
causes.text: From mid-2000 copied games could run from ordinary CDs with no modification to the console.[^19][^20] The proprietary GD-ROM also meant no DVD movies.[^21] How much revenue piracy cost is unknown.

disclaimer: the weights are an interpretive model by the Spectre Brands editors, not a measured quantity. Sega’s reports document the losses. How much each cause contributed is a matter of opinion.
